Siemens Energy triples its dividend and promises €9 billion in share buybacks, powered by electricity grids and gas turbines

On November 11, Siemens Energy closed a record fiscal year and proposed a dividend of €2.30 per share, up from €0.70 a year earlier, along with up to €9 billion in share buybacks by 2030. Lifted by demand for electricity, the stock gained between 6% and 7.8% depending on the source [1][2][3][5].
Net profit for fiscal 2025-2026, which ended in late September, reached €4.129 billion, or €4.44 per share; according to one report, it fell slightly short of analysts’ expectations [1].
The proposed dividend rises to €2.30, from €0.70: it represents roughly half of net profit, excluding one-off items with no cash impact, and still has to be approved by shareholders [1][2].
The group will buy back up to €9 billion of its own shares by fiscal 2030, after €3.1 billion already repurchased in 2025-2026 [1][3].
Its order backlog hit a record €164 billion; orders in the latest quarter, however, came in below the expected €15.47 billion, which the company attributes to the timing of large projects [1].
Siemens Energy is targeting a margin of 20% to 22% before special items by 2030, a goal brought forward [3][4].
Demand is coming from electricity grids and gas turbines, two markets driven by rising power consumption [2].
The stock gained more than 6% according to QNC News, and 7.82% according to another reading from Investing.com; the Stoxx 600 index closed at a record 663.05 points [1][5][6].

Key takeaway: Siemens Energy has more than doubled its profit and is now returning large amounts of money to its shareholders. This success shows how strong demand is for electrical equipment, grids and gas turbines [2][4].
The market chose to look ahead rather than at the quarter: profit slightly below expectations and disappointing quarterly orders did not stop the rise, thanks to the dividend and the buybacks [1].
The €164 billion order backlog represents several years of work already signed, which makes the dividend promises more credible [1].
The session also shows that Europe is riding the AI wave through energy: the day before, Germany’s Infineon had gained more than 5% thanks to the chips that power servers [7].

For you, Siemens Energy illustrates a concrete effect of AI and electrification: makers of turbines and grid equipment are benefiting as much as the tech giants. The group is part of the DAX index, which is held in many European funds. This is not advice to buy or sell.

How it works: why a share buyback lifts the stock price

When a company buys back its own shares, it usually cancels them. Profit is then shared among fewer shares, and each remaining share is entitled to a bigger slice: earnings per share mechanically increase [3]. A buyback also creates a steady buyer on the stock market, which supports demand. Finally, it is a signal: management that promises €9 billion in buybacks over four years is saying it expects to generate a lot of cash, backed here by €164 billion in orders [1][3]. The dividend, for its part, pays money directly to shareholders; Siemens Energy devotes roughly half of its profit to it [2].

In Brazil, Cosan could lift a “poison pill” to sell a stake in rail operator Rumo: both stocks soar

On November 11, the website Brazil Journal reported that the conglomerate Cosan is considering removing a 15% anti-takeover clause to bring an investor into rail operator Rumo, of which it is the largest shareholder. Cosan jumped more than 12% and Rumo 8% on the São Paulo stock exchange [1][2][3].
According to Brazil Journal, Cosan is studying the removal of a “poison pill” that prevents an investor from exceeding 15% of the capital without launching an offer for all the shares [1][6].
The goal: bring strategic investors into Rumo. Talks resumed after the second round of Brazil’s presidential election [1].
Earlier negotiations with Grupo México and with a consortium formed by China’s COFCO and Bunge, covering up to 15% of Rumo, had fallen through [1].
Around 4:40 p.m., Cosan was up 12.39% and Rumo 8.02%, according to Seu Dinheiro [3].
In a statement, Cosan confirmed it is negotiating the sale of part of its stake, but noted that any change to the clause would have to be voted on at an extraordinary general meeting of Rumo [4].

Cosan holds about 20% of Rumo directly and about 10% through swap contracts; some doubt remains over which company’s bylaws contain the clause, as Brazil Journal placed it in Cosan’s bylaws in April [1][2].
The Bovespa index closed up 0.58% that day [7].

Key takeaway: Brazilian rail is attracting buyers from China and Mexico. The candidates already approached, Grupo México and the COFCO-Bunge pair, show that the stakes go beyond the stock market: this is about controlling a key piece of the country’s infrastructure [1][2].

For Cosan, selling a stake in Rumo would bring in cash and reveal the value of its holding: the market is “starting to bet again on unlocking value,” notes Seu Dinheiro, which explains why Cosan is rising more than Rumo [3][5].
The resumption of talks right after the presidential election shows that foreign investors were waiting to know who would hold power before committing to long-term infrastructure [1].
Nothing is settled: the companies have not confirmed the lifting of the clause, and Rumo’s shareholders will have to vote on it [4].

For you, Brazilian rail may seem far away, but Brazil is one of the world’s major agricultural suppliers, and its infrastructure is attracting Chinese and Mexican groups. This race for strategic assets is also playing out in Europe, in ports and energy. This is not advice to buy or sell.

How it works: the “poison pill,” a clause that protects or blocks

A poison pill is a rule written into a company’s bylaws: if an investor crosses a threshold, here 15% of the capital, it must buy all the shares or face consequences that make the deal very costly [1][6]. It is meant to prevent a creeping, cheap takeover. But it also discourages a partner that only wants a large minority stake [6]. Lifting it opens the door to new buyers: that is why the stock rises, as investors anticipate a sale at a good price [2][3]. In Brazil, this change must be voted on by shareholders at a general meeting [4].

After the ruling, Airgas stock fell more than 4%, to around $61 [10][11].

Twitter adopts a one-year pill, triggered above 15% of the capital, while Elon Musk holds about 9% and offers about $43 billion [9].
The board specified that it did not prevent it from considering an offer in the shareholders’ interest [9].

Wendy’s rejects the $1.4 billion offer from Nelson Peltz’s Trian fund and adopts a one-year pill [8].
Unlike Cosan’s case, the pill here serves to fend off a buyer; lifting it at Rumo would serve to attract one [1][8].

Fund manager GQG Partners plunges 25% in two days in Sydney: $6.7 billion pulled by clients after a failed bet on tech

On November 11, Sydney-listed asset manager GQG Partners revealed that its clients had withdrawn $6.7 billion in October, after a risky shift by its founder Rajiv Jain toward technology stocks. The stock fell 19.6%, then another 6.4% on Thursday, to 73 Australian cents [1][3].
GQG’s assets under management shrank by about $17.7 billion in one month, to $131.6 billion at the end of October [1].
The decline came from $6.7 billion in net client withdrawals and $11.0 billion in investment losses [1].
October’s withdrawals were almost triple those of September ($2.3 billion); they mainly hit the emerging markets fund ($3.2 billion) and the international fund ($2.2 billion) [2].
Since January, clients have withdrawn about $32.9 billion, and assets have fallen about 24% from their February peak of $172.9 billion [1][2].
In July, the flagship Global Equity fund shifted toward technology and semiconductor stocks; it lost more than 10% in October as AI stocks tumbled [2].
The stock lost 19.6%, to A$0.78, on Wednesday, then another 6.4%, to 73 cents, on Thursday; it is down 42.5% over twelve months [1][2][3].
Rajiv Jain defends his choice: there is “nothing to regret,” because “the data is so strong” in favor of tech [2].
Key takeaway: a fund manager lives on the fees charged on the money it manages. When clients leave and investments fall at the same time, its future revenue drops, and its stock along with it [1][2].
The GQG case shows how the slump in AI stocks in early November is spreading far beyond Silicon Valley, all the way to the Australian stock market [2][4].
The timing is brutal: GQG moved into tech in July, near the peak, and took the full force of the October-November correction [2].
On Thursday, the Sydney stock market also fell, with the S&P/ASX 200 index down 0.5% in the morning, at 9,110.9 points, after reports about the future of Nvidia’s CEO [4].

For you, this episode is a reminder that an actively managed fund can lose a lot when its manager bets on a sector at the wrong time. Before choosing a fund, look at its strategy, its fees and how it has weathered downturns. This is not advice to buy or sell.

How it works: a fund manager’s double whammy

An asset manager like GQG charges a percentage of the money it manages every year. Its revenue therefore depends on two things: the money clients entrust to it and the value of the investments [1]. In October, both fell at the same time: $6.7 billion in withdrawals and $11.0 billion in market losses [1]. The cycle can become vicious: poor performance drives clients away, and withdrawals force the sale of securities. Investors anticipate this drop in future revenue, which explains why the stock is falling harder than assets under management, which fell about 12% in one month [1][2].

news.2026-11-12-pays-bas-box-3-taxe-mill: Netherlands: two governing parties team up with the left to tax large fortunes more heavily, without the VVD

On Wednesday, November 11, D66 and the CDA, two of the three parties in Rob Jetten’s government, reached an agreement with two opposition parties, PRO and Volt, on a scaled-back version of their “millionaires’ tax.” The VVD (liberals), the third partner, opposes it. The vote was scheduled for Thursday, November 12 [1][2].
The idea: shift about €1 billion in taxes from wealth to income from work, through a new rate for the richest in “box 3,” which taxes savings and investments [2][3].
The box 3 rate would rise to 35.5%, and to 38.5% above €60,000 in gains, compared with 45% in the original plan [4].
With D66 and the CDA, the amendment appears to have a majority in both chambers even without the VVD; PRO and Volt would then vote for the tax plan [1].
The VVD considers the measure contrary to the coalition agreement and fears it will drive away entrepreneurs and investors [1][2].
Key takeaway: the Jetten government has a majority in neither the House nor the Senate, and without opposition support for its tax plan, it would lose nearly €2.5 billion in revenue next year [2][5].
The three parties can vote differently on certain bills: according to coalition sources, the VVD is not expected to leave the government [1].
For you, taxing large fortunes is also a debate in France: here, a compromise passes thanks to an alternative majority.

South Korea: record 1.6 trillion won fine for 15 banks and brokers that colluded on government debt

South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission (FTC) announced on Wednesday, November 11, a total fine of about 1.62 trillion won ($1.2 billion) against 15 financial institutions. They colluded in government bond auctions for more than three years. It is the heaviest penalty in its history [1][2].

The 15 firms penalized, 10 brokerages and 5 banks, are government debt “primary dealers.” They exchanged information on the rates and volumes they bid in 150 auctions, from January 2020 to June 2023 [1][3].
In 145 auctions, they set specific rates or volumes [1]. KB Securities received the largest fine, 332.1 billion won, ahead of NH Investment & Securities, at 242.7 billion [1].
Seven institutions, including Mirae Asset Securities, IBK bank and the Korea Development Bank, have been referred for criminal prosecution [1].
The fine was calculated on 54 trillion won in bonds won at auction; the institutions dispute this basis, making an appeal likely [6].
Key takeaway: government bonds serve as a benchmark for setting interest rates and pricing other financial products; that is why the FTC calls it a serious violation [1].
The previous record, 1.03 trillion won, targeted Qualcomm in 2016 [1]. The Seoul Economic Daily calls for care not to disrupt the market where the government finances itself [5].
For you, it is a reminder: government borrowing rates serve as the basis for loans, so rigging these auctions affects everyone.

news.2026-11-12-mexique-budget-2027-depu: Mexico: lawmakers pass a 10.6 trillion peso 2027 budget and trim the electoral authority’s funding

Mexico’s Chamber of Deputies passed the 2027 federal budget overnight from November 10 to 11, after a session of about 20 hours: 10.636 trillion pesos in spending, or 1.3% more than in 2026 after inflation. The National Electoral Institute (INE) loses 6 billion pesos [2][3][4].
The bill passed by 352 votes to 130, with no abstentions, and was then sent to the executive branch [1][3].
The majority accepted none of the opposition’s proposals: the Budget Committee’s draft passed without changes [2][3].
The 6 billion taken from the INE go in particular to the school program “La Escuela es Nuestra” (3 billion), the environment (1 billion) and the search for missing persons (300 million) [2][4].
Planned public investment amounts to about 1.13 trillion pesos [3].
Key takeaway: the INE organizes elections; cutting its budget ahead of next year’s vote is a sensitive issue, amid debate over the institution’s independence [2][5].
President Claudia Sheinbaum welcomed the transfers to health, schools and the environment and said next year’s elections are “guaranteed” with the budget granted to the INE [5].
For you, Mexico is a major trading partner of Europe and a country where many French companies have production: how it manages its finances and its elections matters for their stability.

news.2026-11-12-japon-tva-alimentation-1: Japan: the cut in the food tax, from 8% to 1%, reaches the upper house, where Takaichi has no majority

Japan’s upper house began reviewing Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s bill on Wednesday, November 11: the consumption tax on food and non-alcoholic beverages would drop from 8% to 1% for two years starting in April 2027, along with an income-linked cash payment [3][4].
The ruling coalition is 4 seats short of a majority in the upper house; the key question is which opposition demands it will accept [1].
Sanae Takaichi repeated that the cash payment would target “at least 30%” of working people and wants households to “feel” the relief [2][3].
On November 6, the lower house passed the bill with the LDP and the Innovation Party; the entire opposition voted against it, and former Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba left before the vote [4][5].
If the upper house rejects it, the lower house can override with a two-thirds vote; the government is aiming for passage in December [5].
Key takeaway: the measure is expensive for a country that is already heavily indebted, and the opposition criticizes the government for not saying how it will pay for it [5][6].
It has until the end of the year to explain how it will pay for the tax cut and the increase in military spending; according to Bloomberg, some options would bypass budget safeguards [6].
For you, if Tokyo finances this cut with more debt, Japanese interest rates and the yen could move, and with them the cost of a trip to Japan.
Final passage targeted by the government and the ruling majority [5].

news.2026-11-12-inde-subvention-engrais-: India: the Modi government boosts fertilizer aid by 64%, at the heart of a 771 billion rupee package

India’s cabinet approved five measures worth 77,101 crore rupees (771 billion) on Wednesday, November 11. The largest: 62,370 crore in fertilizer subsidies for the 2026-2027 winter crop season, up 64% [1][2].
The fertilizer subsidy rises by 24,417.73 crore compared with the previous winter season; the government attributes this to higher global prices for fertilizers and their raw materials [2][3].
The Aqua Line of the Noida metro, in the Delhi suburbs, will be extended by 8.45 km to Greater Noida, with five elevated stations, for 2,390 crore [1].
Two credit guarantee funds for small businesses receive 5,000 crore (MUDRA loans to micro-enterprises) and 4,111 crore (Stand-Up India program) [1].
A museum, the “Yuge Yugeen Bharat,” will be set up in the North and South Block buildings in New Delhi for 3,230 crore [1][5].
Key takeaway: the Indian state covers a large share of the price of fertilizers to protect farmers; when global prices rise, the public bill climbs [2][3].
With the credit guarantees, New Delhi is also seeking to make it easier for micro and small businesses to access credit [1][4].
For you, the increase in this subsidy is a signal: global fertilizer prices remain high, which also weighs on European farmers’ costs and, at the end of the chain, on food prices.

news.2026-11-12-italie-alertes-bombe-630: Italy: thousands of schools targeted by hoax bomb threats, including a threat against Giorgia Meloni

On Wednesday, November 11, about 6,300 Italian schools received emails announcing a bomb, according to Reuters; at least 300 were evacuated. The message also threatened Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. Similar threats targeted the United Kingdom and Ireland [1][2].
The email claimed that an explosive device had been placed in Giorgia Meloni’s car [4].
It was signed “Mikhail Andropov, head of the Vilayat of Misoginistan,” a made-up name [5].
The government called a meeting of ministers [1]. Giorgia Meloni said the threats posed no danger and that the police were monitoring the situation [2][5].
Similar messages reached schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland; Russia and Iran deny any involvement [2][3].
Key takeaway: these waves of threats paralyze schools and public services at little cost, and they have been recurring across Europe in recent weeks [3].
Accusations often point to hostile states, but with no public evidence so far: Moscow and Tehran deny it [2].
For you, France has also seen threats of this kind in recent days: they are costly in evacuations and lost hours, even when they are fake.

news.2026-11-12-belgique-de-wever-budget: Belgium: De Wever seeks an “armistice” on a €10 billion budget, as people removed from unemployment benefits add to the bill

Kept in office by King Philippe, who refused his resignation on November 6, Prime Minister Bart De Wever is trying to secure an agreement on the 2027 budget among the five parties in his coalition. The targeted effort is €10 billion; he must report to the king on Monday, November 16 [1][2].
The king’s refusal settles nothing: he asked Bart De Wever to resume talks, with no agreement so far on the 2027 budget [2].
Since November 10, the Prime Minister has been holding one-on-one meetings with the coalition leaders, including Frank Vandenbroucke, and has canceled his European trips [3][4].
A new expense is weighing on the accounts: €208 million linked to unemployed people removed from benefits who are turning to the CPAS, the municipal social welfare centers [1].
This extra cost adds to the overrun in the 2026 budget [1].
Key takeaway: Belgium’s budget crisis, triggered by Bart De Wever’s resignation in early November, is not over: the king is awaiting his report and no agreement has been reached [1][2].
The shift of people removed from unemployment benefits to the CPAS shows that part of the spending is sliding from the federal state to local social welfare, further widening the 2026 deficit [1].
For you, Belgium is a neighbor and a major trading partner of France: a prolonged political crisis in Brussels can delay European decisions and worry lenders.
